author: A total of 70 genomes were considered for inclusion (Table S1). The candidate panel was composed of 69 cynipoid genomes and one outgroup, *Telenomus remus* (Platygastroidea: Scelionidae). In addition to the new *Euceroptres primus* genome (S1), a set of 40 cynipoid assemblies and *T. remus* were downloaded from NCBI in October 2025\. Additionally, whole-genome DNA reads were downloaded from ENA (18) and NCBI (1) and assembled using SPAdes v3.15.5 (Bankevich et al. 2012). Finally, an additional 9 assemblies were downloaded from NCBI in July 2026\. Of these, we chose *Belonocnema kinseyi* (NCBI accession GCF\_010883055.1) as our reference genome. This accession was originally uploaded as *Belonocnema treatae*, before the Texas population from which the samples were collected was re-described as *B. kinseyi* (Zhang et al. 2021). In order to verify the absence of each gene family in the ancestors of Cynipoidea, we also downloaded 15 protein sets for a representative panel of Hymenoptera and Diptera. These were used for whole genome protein detection only and excluded from chromosome-scale analysis. BUSCO v6.0 was used to evaluate the completeness of genomes relative to the hymenoptera\_odb12 protein set (Tegenfeldt et al. 2025). Since only three of the genomes (*B. kinseyi*, *Leptopilina boulardi* and *L. heterotoma*) were previously annotated, Helixer v0.3.6 (model invertebrate\_v0.3\_m\_0100; Stiehler et al. 2021\) was used to predict genomic elements. NCBI annotations were retained only for *B. kinseyi*. Of the genomes we considered, 12 were removed because they fell below a 40% BUSCO completeness threshold. Taxonomic redundancy (8) and other assembly quality issues (1) prompted the removal of another 9 genomes, resulting in a core analytic set of 49 annotated genomes (Table S1).

author: We found 77 flanking gene patterns could be matched across more than one genome (Table S5). Of these, 26 contained target genes in two or more genomes, accounting for 68.5% (463/676) of genome-derived target loci. The modal GH5\_2 block on chromosome 10 was recovered in 38/49 genomes; 26 contained at least one GH5\_2 gene and 12 were empty. The modal GH5\_2 block on chromosome 6 was recovered in 45/49 genomes; 22 contained at least one GH5\_2 gene and 23 were empty. The modal PL1\_8 block on chromosome 8 was recovered in 43/49 genomes, including 27 with PL1\_8 and 16 empty. The modal PL4\_4 block on chromosome 7 was recovered in 37/49 genomes, including 27 with PL4\_4 and 10 empty. The modal B-lectin block on chromosome 6 was recovered in 45/49 genomes, including 17 with B-lectin and 28 empty.

author: Because introns do not occur in bacteria, the presence of an intron is strong evidence that a gene is incorporated into the cynipoid genome. While introns are preferentially placed near the end of signal peptides in secreted genes (Tordai and Patthy 2004), their precise placement and phase provide an independent line of evidence to trace the history of a bacterial gene after its insertion. All three PCWDE families contain introns (Figure 3; Table S9), and both phase and placement relative to CDS are conserved within each PCWDE family, indicating that all candidate proteins from each family were the result of a single transfer. Modal intron positions are shared across paralogs regardless of chromosome placement. Among proteins with coherent single-scaffold CDS models, 87.5% (154/176) of GH5\_2 paralogs have an intron at reference amino acid position 18, including 58 placed on chromosome 6 and 52 on chromosome 10\. 41.5% (88/212) of PL1\_8 paralogs contain an intron at reference amino acid position 9\. 39.5% (85/215) of PL4\_4 paralogs have an intron at reference amino acid position 83, and an additional 14.9% (32/215) have one at position 37\. In each case, the modal intron is found in all cynipoid families where the gene is present. Introns in all three PCWDEs are strongly biased toward the N terminus, consistent with a bias toward the signal peptide: 85.1% of introns were observed within the first quarter of the CDS, compared with 32.4% for all genes. The median relative position of PCWDE introns was 5.5% of the way through the CDS; the genome-wide median was 44.2%.

author: Intron placement was less informative for B-lectin genes. Only 21.4% (6/28) of genome-derived B-lectin genes contain any introns. However, incomplete gene models due to inconsistent annotation by Helixer may limit intron discovery, and the loss of the majority of the gene in its chromosome 3 duplication prevents the use of intron placement to independently validate its homology with the chromosome 6 occurrence.

author: Bacterial and eukaryotic genomes have different baseline nucleotide frequencies, and over time, transferred sequences are expected to drift toward the nucleotide frequency of the recipient. While coding bases are constrained by selection, the third base in each codon can vary more freely because changes there are often synonymous. Therefore, the proportion of G and C at the third position of each codon (GC3) can indicate a shift from bacterial baseline to eukaryotic baseline. Within bacteria, all three PCWDE gene families show widely varied rates of GC3 %, with medians above 50%. Wasp genes have a much lower baseline GC3 frequency, with a median of 36% (Table S8). After acquisition by cynipoids, all three gene families now resemble the wasp genome baseline. By family, wasp paralogs of GH5\_2, PL1\_8, and PL4\_4 are 2.0 percentage points above, 4.3 below, and 2.4 below the wasp median, respectively, while their closely related bacterial lineages are considerably higher at 17.7, 19.2, and 15.8 percentage points above. For the B-lectin, wasp paralogs are 11.1 pp above the wasp gene median while closely related bacterial lineages are 56.9 pp above. Full statistics are presented in supplementary text S7.

author: Some genomes may contain evidence of bacterial genes too degraded to recover in annotation. To detect these pseudogene fragments, a representative sequence for each gene family was used as a tblastn v2.16.0+ (Camacho et al. 2009\) query against all 49 retained, 21 excluded, and 5 alternate assemblies. To avoid false positives, tblastn hits above a 45% identity floor and family-specific overlap length thresholds (supplementary text S3) were treated as provisional and results were evaluated only for genome-gene family combinations lacking an accepted Helixer/dbCAN family member. HSP findings were queried against CynOGs and hits that didn’t match the corresponding PCWDE gene were removed. Hits below the 45% identity floor were considered as possible pseudogenes only where other hits for that family and genome were not found. Pseudogene status was assigned based on the presence of reading frame disruptions and premature stop codons.

author: PacBio HiFi sequencing yielded a highly contiguous genome for *Euceroptres primus*. From one Revio cell where the barcoded *E. primus* SMRTBell library represented one third of the sequencing run, 2,706,303 HiFi reads (37.95 Gb of HiFi data) were obtained, of which 30 (0.0011% of reads) were discarded after filtering with HiFiAdapterFilt. The genome coverage was estimated at 44.6× coverage as reported by GenomeScope2.

author: A total of 14 Trinity assemblies were generated (Table S1), with a wide range of read counts and assembly qualities (protein BUSCO completeness 36.5-93.4%). Transcriptomes were only used to contribute to gene phylogenies and not to support claims about chromosome position or gene loss, so we did not apply a minimum coverage threshold. Read-sorting identified two larval samples with predominant hits to chalcidoid genomes, which were removed from analysis. Three kinds of cynipid larvae are found within Cynipini galls, including the Cynipini inducer and *Ceroptres* and *Synergus* inquilines. Read-sorting allowed us to construct three *Synergus* assemblies (from galls of *Belonocnema kinseyi,* *Druon quercuslanigerum,* and *Druon ignotum*) and one *Ceroptres* assembly (from galls of *Druon ignotum)*. Trinity assemblies and predicted proteins were generated for Synergini: *Synergus* ex *Belonocnema kinseyi, Synergus* ex *Druon ignotum*, *Synergus* ex *Druon quercuslanigerum*; Ceroptresini: *Ceroptres* ex *Druon ignotum;* and Cynipini: *Callirhytis quercusbatatoides, Disholcaspis cinerosa, Neuroterus howertoni*, *Andricus quercusfoliatus,* *Druon ignotum, Bassettia pallida, Dryocosmus quercuspalustris*, *Biorhiza pallida*, *Neuroterus numismalis,* and *Neuroterus quercusbaccarum.*

author: Some genomes may contain evidence of bacterial genes too degraded to recover in annotation. To detect these pseudogene fragments, a representative sequence for each gene family was used as a tblastn v2.16.0+ (E-value \< 1e-5, SEG filtering enabled, max 200 targets; Camacho et al. 2009\) query against all 75 assemblies, including retained, alternate, and excluded assemblies. To avoid false positives, tblastn hits were treated as provisional and results were evaluated only for genome-gene family combinations lacking an accepted Helixer/dbCAN family member. For GH5\_2, PL1\_8, and PL4\_4, candidate HSPs were required to overlap the focal query domain by at least 150, 150, and 250 amino acids, respectively, and to have at least 45% amino-acid identity. B-lectin candidates were required to derive from a non-plant query, align for at least 90 amino acids, have a bit score of at least 120, and have at least 40% identity. Finally, HSP findings were queried against CynOGs and hits that didn’t match the corresponding PCWDE gene were removed. We found only one case for which a gene family was represented in a genome only by a pseudogene. *Parnips nigripes* contains a PL1\_8-like region whose tblastn hits fell below the 45% identity threshold, which was characterized separately by protein-to-genome alignment of two cynipid PL1\_8 proteins (*Aulacidea tavakolii* and *Ceroptres masudai*) with miniprot v0.9 and exonerate v2.4.0 (protein2genome), followed by a dbCAN-sub hmmsearch of the translated alignment.

author: After deduplication, our outgroup screens identified 306 total PCWDE outgroup sequences (Table S3). For PL1\_8, we found 57 bacterial sequences and 6 non-cynipoid eukaryote sequences (3 Cecidomyiidae, 2 Apidae, 1 Oomycota). For PL4\_4, we found 64 bacterial sequences and 13 non-cynipoid eukaryote sequences (6 fungus, 4 *Cuscuta*, 3 Coleoptera). For GH5\_2, we found 154 bacterial sequences and 12 non-cynipoid eukaryote sequences (9 Nematoda, 2 Protista, 1 Coleoptera). We found 35 bacterial PI-PLC-X sequences. For GH30\_3, we found 122 bacteria and 66 non-cynipoid eukaryote sequences (40 fungus, 20 metazoa, 5 rotifer, 1 plant). For B-lectin, we found 112 bacteria and 160 non-cynipoid eukaryote sequences (68 plant, 38 fungus, 36 metazoa, 18 rotifer). However, only one outgroup sequence contained the full intact domain architecture including PI-PLC-X, GH30\_3, and tandem B-lectin: bacterial species *Actinoplanes awajinensis*.

author: To build alignments for phylogenetic trees, cynipoid and outgroup protein sequences were filtered to remove incomplete or unusually long gene predictions. The final domain-trimmed analysis sets contained 427 GH5\_2 sequences (261 cynipoid, 166 outgroup; median length 318 aa), 365 PL1\_8 sequences (302 cynipoid, 63 outgroup; median 294 aa), and 446 PL4\_4 sequences (367 cynipoid, 79 outgroup; median 555 aa) (Table S3). B-lectin sequences were processed separately to accommodate domain diversity. Of 67 cynipoid B-lectin-family proteins identified, 48 contained at least one intact B-lectin domain. Because some proteins contributed up to four B-lectin domains, and because two domains from the domain-complete representative bacterium *Actinoplanes awajinensis* were included, 69 trimmed B-lectin domains were used for phylogenetic analysis. Catalytic-domain sets were constructed independently and included 204 GH30\_3 (16 cynipoid and 188 outgroup) and 42 PI-PLC-X domains (7 cynipoid and 35 bacterial).

author: To generate both sets of phylogenies, sequences were aligned with MAFFT v7 (Katoh and Standley 2013). Maximum-likelihood protein trees were inferred with IQ-TREE v3.0.1 (Wong et al. 2026\) under a fixed LG+G4 model. Branch support was estimated with 1,000 UFBoot2 replicates (-B 1000; Hoang et al. 2018). Cynipoid locus trees (Figure S5; Figure 4 panels are pruned from them) were inferred from the copies in all 49 panel genomes, using the best-E-value domain-overlap rule, together with transcript tips from Trinity assemblies of *Neuroterus numismalis*, *N. quercusbaccarum,* and *Biorhiza pallida* larvae. Each family's tree was rooted on the bacterial sequence with the smallest mean patristic distance to the cynipoid tips in the transfer-context tree. The final trees contain 255 GH5\_2, 294 PL1\_8 and 358 PL4\_4 cynipoid tips plus that outgroup. Four *Bassettia pallida* transcript-derived sequences (one PL1\_8, two PL4\_4 and one B-lectin) were 99.1–100% identical in aligned protein sequence to *Callirhytis quercusbatatoides* sequences and lay 0.000–0.014 substitutions/site from them, so they were attributed to *C. quercusbatatoides*. They were pruned from the transfer-context and B-lectin trees after inference and were excluded before inference from the locus trees.

author: Two methods were used to determine whether members of each gene family were found in consistent genomic regions of different species. Our primary method was to use RagTag to align all scaffolds from all non-chromosome scale genomes to the 10 chromosome-scale scaffolds of the GCF\_010883055.1 *B. kinseyi* assembly, numbered by length in decreasing order, as reference (Alonge 2022). For *Euceroptres primus,* which was assembled to 6 chromosome-scale scaffolds, and for *Dryocosmus kuriphilus*, which was assembled to 10 chromosomes (Liu et al. 2024), JCVI v1.5.11 was used to assign target genes to *B. kinseyi*\-chromosome-equivalent regions (Tang et al. 2024). Because reference-guided scaffolding can join fragments across chromosomal boundaries, references to chromosomes 1-10 refer to genomic blocks based on the 10 *B. kinseyi* pseudochromosomes and are used as a coordinate system rather than statements about karyotype.

author: Our second method was to examine the flanking genes surrounding each target gene. This analysis also allowed us to validate that genes for each target family are integrated into cynipoid genomes and rule out bacterial sequences included due to assembly errors. First, genomes were annotated with Helixer (S2) and masked for repeats. RepeatModeler v2.0.7 was used to create a per-genome library of repetitive elements (Flynn et al. 2020). This library was deduplicated, filtered to remove known genes, and used to guide RepeatMasker v4.2.2 softmasking of all genomes (Smit et al. 2013-2015). An orthology catalog was initially constructed from 667,137 proteins from 41 genome proteomes after excluding proteins for which at least 30% of CDS bases were repeat-masked. Proteins were assigned to orthogroups, designated CynOGs, with OrthoFinder v2.5.5 in orthogroups-only mode (-og), using DIAMOND for sequence search (-S diamond; Buchfink et al. 2021), 32 search and analysis threads (-t 32 \-a 32), and MCL inflation 1.5 (van Dongen 2000). After merging co-linear gene-model fragments, proteins with at least 15% repeat overlap were removed from orthogroups represented in five or fewer genomes; orthogroups left without members were discarded. This produced 22,448 CynOGs containing 623,796 proteins. Profile HMMs were constructed for CynOGs containing at least three members. Sequences were aligned with MAFFT v7.526 (--auto; Katoh and Standley 2013), trimmed with trimAl (-automated1; Capella-Gutiérrez et al. 2009), and converted to profile HMMs with HMMER 3.4 hmmbuild (Eddy 2011), yielding 17,928 profiles. A self-recovery check using hmmsearch assigned 99 of 100 randomly selected source proteins to the correct CynOG, and the profile library was indexed with hmmpress. Proteins from nine later-added or replacement proteomes as well as proteins predicted from transcriptomes were searched against this library at E \< 1 × 10⁻⁵ and assigned to the CynOG with the best full-sequence E-value and score.

author: After shared synteny blocks were defined, we looked for each conserved flanking gene pattern across all 49 genomes. We filtered the flanking gene set to only those present in more than 50% of block members and looked for occurrences clustered within 500 kb. After a synteny block was identified, we rescanned all gene models within the search region for target hits, including tblastn hits. When a match was discovered, the genome contained a target hit at that locus, and the number of tandem repeats was counted; if it didn’t, the locus was marked EMPTY. If fewer than 3 conserved flanking genes could be found in a cluster, the block was marked NOT\_DETERMINED for that genome.

author: To determine whether the rate of paralog retention and chromosome translocation of bacterially derived PCWDEs were exceptional, we compared them to baseline rates among CAZymes in cynipoid genomes. Because dbCAN subfamilies are manually defined and may subdivide better-studied groups more finely, biasing copy number, we used eCAMI sequence clusters, which are subdivided computationally using a threshold of sequence similarity (Xu et al. 2020). The largest eCAMI cluster corresponding to our prior dbCAN sub membership in each genome was used as the target gene representative for comparison. For lineage summaries, genomes were grouped as Cynipini (12 genomes), other Cynipidae (22), Diplolepididae (3) and *Euceroptres primus* (1). We report the median rank and percentile per lineage in Table S6.

author: For each eCAMI cluster, we reconstructed chromosome occupancy using RagTag placements and the species tree presented in Figure S2, with assignments adjudicated by parsimony (DELTRAN; Fitch 1971\) and counted inferred gains of chromosome placement. Because groups present in more genomes are represented more broadly in the tree, gains were expressed per genome. The PCWDE families were compared with the 227 non-PCWDE clusters present at the cynipoid crown in at least five genomes, both overall and within clusters of similar median copy number (Table S7).

author: To obtain a baseline rate of intron placement, we conducted a second scan using distinct methods. For each gene, the transcript with the longest CDS was used, and transcripts whose CDS features spanned more than one scaffold or strand were excluded. Introns were defined as gaps between consecutive CDS features, as for the PCWDE copies. Because background genes share no common reference protein, intron positions were not aligned or clustered; instead, each intron was assigned a relative position equal to the fraction of the CDS preceding it, measured in nucleotides from the start codon. The same method was applied to the PCWDE introns for comparison. The background comprised 2,911,604 introns in 649,754 genes and was summarized as the fraction of introns in the first quarter of the CDS and the median relative position. Target-family genes (631) were not removed from the background. This baseline places 32.4% of all introns in the first quarter of their gene, while 85.1% of PCWDE introns fall in the first quarter of their gene.

author: Nucleotide frequency was assessed only at the third codon position (GC3), because this site is more likely to be synonymous and therefore faces reduced stabilizing selection. For each genome, we calculated a background GC3 distribution from the longest coding sequence of every annotated gene. GC3 was measured for 603 PCWDE copies and 28 B-lectin copies, and each copy was ranked by its percentile of the background rate in its genome. Using the transfer-context tree (S4), we chose the closest sampled bacterial relatives of the cynipoid members of each gene family and evaluated their GC3. For each genome and gene family, we calculated the median absolute difference in percentage points between wasp copies and the genome background median, and between bacterial relatives and the genome background median. The two values were compared across species with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (37, 37 and 36 species for GH5\_2, PL1\_8 and PL4\_4; 16 for B-lectin; Table S8). Wasp copies lay within 2.6–4.4 percentage points of their host-genome GC3 median, versus 16.7–19.2 points for their closest bacterial relatives (Wilcoxon signed-rank P \< 10⁻¹⁰ for each family; B-lectin 11 vs 57 points, P \= 3 × 10⁻⁵).

author:
B-lectin is found with its full domain structure intact on chromosome 6 in nearly all cynipid tribes, indicating this is the original placement. An additional placement on chromosome 3 is limited to Cynipini and contains only one intact B-lectin domain. Several translocations to nonmodal positions occurred in each family (Figures 1 and S2). *Eschatocerus acaciae,* a cynipoid with inconsistent placement in previous phylogenies but placed as basal to Cynipidae in Hearn et al. (2024), shares the modal cynipid chromosome placements for GH5\_2 and PL4\_4, though its PL1\_8 is unplaced and it lacks the bacterial B-lectin. This is congruent with its published placement in Cynipidae, and suggests the acquisition of B-lectin occurred after its divergence.   
   
To identify true orthologous loci within each family and to verify the absence of genes in lineages where the target proteins weren’t found, we compared flanking gene sequences adjacent to each occurrence of each gene to identify blocks of conserved synteny. A total of 77 flanking gene patterns could be matched across more than one genome (Table S5). Of these, 26 contained target genes in two or more genomes, accounting for 68.5% (463/676) of genome-derived target loci. Target genes in many synteny loci occur in tandem duplications, up to a maximum of 10 per locus. In many cases, synteny blocks recovered by our criteria as independent are found in relatively close proximity; six PL1\_8 blocks were separated by fewer than 20 genes. Synteny blocks were also detected in species lacking target genes, marked as empty in Table S5, giving strong evidence that absence of the gene in those species indicates a block predates insertion or postdates loss, rather than poor assembly quality. Species taxonomically closer to *B. kinseyi* recovered more flanking genes per locus and synteny blocks were less likely to be undetectable even in poor quality assemblies. In the most distant species, the outgroup platygastroid *T. remus*, only 24/77 cross-genome-detected synteny blocks were recovered, all of which lacked the target protein, supporting the inference that the transfer happened after the divergence of Cynipoidea and Platygastroidea.
